title: The anti AI game dev argument seems to be retreating to "You cant be bothered to make a good game"
author: Tom_Baron
selftext:
Im seeing less and less "Claude writes dangerous, obsolete and messy code" posts and more and more "you simply dont have the judgement, knowledge or persistence to execute a production grade game" posts. 

What if some of us are happy to iterate on our projects for months? Claude wont build a perfect game in a week, thats for sure, but if you know how an element should work/look/feel, itll get there via iteration and lots of iterations on every aspect of a game, tied by an underlying vision of what you are trying to achieve will likely bring some great products to life. 

Chances are the games that have really had the work put in on are simply not ready yet.

comments.author: MrNotmark
comments.body:
I'm not sure if claude can build a finished game by itself honestly.
I've seen people try to build a simple boss fight, and it costed the user 400 dollars and it was building that fight for 12 hours. (With fable)
It looked epic and yes it was with fable and not opus 5.5 but i think you would have somewhat similar experience.
I also think that Claude would just use generic mechanics that are simply not interesting enough, it does not have creativity on its own and you have to hold its hand, tell it exactly what you want at in detail.

So in a way I think that's what people argue about, but if you iterate with claude and hold its hand and refine every tiny detail, then yes I think you can make a pretty good game. But at that point you also have to understand gamedev and the engine and its limitations

replies.author: FazedEclipse2
replies.body:
Build in ChatGPT and you get what it thinks is good, clean crisp ui modern fonts, all the buttons on screen like your 5, a completeable game not a challenging one.

Build in Claude and its better but needs work. You have to specify what you want, give examples of the look and style, this one prompt madness is a load of nonsense if you are serious.

But spending hours on a boss fight? I would assume the boss fight relies on mechanics in the full game, build to the boss fight and suddenly all the tools are ready to apply.

replies.author: MrNotmark
replies.body:
I doubt it's that simple, a whole game requires much more mechanics than a singular boss fight
Inventory, level up skills,, travel and most of the map is missing 
Also do you think the ai could make the game without knowing anything about the code?

replies.author: FazedEclipse2
replies.body:
What do you mean? You start the build with a full plan or you hatch it out with a planning session.

You dont start the build until that plan is in place. Once its in place thats it, dont make any changes to the plan, playtest yourself find the "fun" factor, if its not there thats where you tell the ai what needs to change. By the time it comes to your specifically detailed boss fight, you have everything planned and built to get you there.

replies.author: MrNotmark
replies.body:
Yeah right, in my experience the bigger area you give the ai the worse the game becomes. For example I gave astra unlimited budget once and let it build the entire world map for me and the UI,  and I even gave it a detailed spec but I think it failed miserably because the scope was too big, or maybe I'm just a bad prompter?
I think when you give something to the AI it will try to do it in the most easy way possible and it wants to follow the path of least resistance, which makes sense when you realise that it was mostly trained on smaller scope problems rather than big ones.
I much prefer to feed it small problems at a time and understand it step by step

replies.author: FazedEclipse2
replies.body: Yeah you dont one shot it. You plan out each step with a good planner model then you go at it one step at a time testing checking as you go

comments.author: Fun-Term616
comments.body:
I see that and I don't like posts like that. I've been a developer for a long time and I'm just amazed by what people are doing with no skill in coding. It's brand new tech and we are in the figuring-it-out stage. Most of these games probably will never be finished or be fun. Most games aren't fun and that's been happening long before AI. A lot of people have spent years on a game that never got released or nobody liked it. 
The devops team I was on, our motto was "fail fast". You can do that with ai. You can get a game up and running in a month. So even if it sucks it's not that big of a deal. I believe it's 90% of code written has never been used. It's called shelfware. In my lifetime 95% of the stuff I've written has never been used. So who cares about the criticism. I like seeing people post their ideas and games. I don't care if it's creative or not. The novelty of ai still impresses me.

comments.author: lin_dhu
comments.body:
I don't know why but I feel like every AI post seem to miss the mark when it comes to the pushback of AI in game design spaces.

I genuinely don't know how to explain, but telling claude to redo and change elements of the code until it looks like the vision you had in mind feels like the wrong way to go about it

If you have a vision, then you should also know how it works. If you keep claude to re-iterate until it finally gets your "vision", chances are your game isn't a great product that needs to come to life.

And so far no ai vibecoded project proved me wrong. People keep saying ai allows people with great ideas bring their vision to life and yet I haven't seen an example of this.

replies.author: ByerN
replies.body:
Let's take a look at it from my perspective as a non-casual player (casuals are a different story).

It is much harder now to look for games compared to the time before the LLM boom. All of the subs where I was looking for games are useless now. Next Fest and other big Steam festivals, too.

I had to fall back to influencers on YT, but their throughput is limited because of the YT algorithm punishing many uploads per day, so I am missing games they don't cover because of their limited time. The solution is to look for more niche influencers, but the whole burden is moved more and more towards the player making it harder to find good games. 

To make their life easier, non-casual players who actively look for new games to play (like myself) are sceptical of games with AI graphics (AI code is not required in the disclosure) or are filtering out games with AI disclosure entirely, causing some shady AI devs not to disclose AI and getting negative reviews when someone finds it out.

Steam sees the issue and is trying to fix it with a personal calendar and new changes to the upcoming Steam Next Fest, but it is relatively new.

From my perspective, the whole process of finding games I'd like to play is worse than it was before, and I am not alone. 

You can say that "huh, but there was human-slop before AI", but the problem is the scale of the issue. It is comparable to the wave of asset flips years ago, when we were flooded with asset-flip quick cash-grabs, but it is much worse now. A lot of people back then hated games made in Unity solely because of it.

replies.author: senseven

There is tons of hard stuff in there.

I work in media, I occasionally have lunch with writers, musicians, directors. That grind is their day by day since forever. Its always press, curators, streamers, "best releases this month". Anything to punch through the noise. Gamers and game devs maybe had it a touch easier, but I don't think so. Film makers compete with shot and gun people doing "movies" on the very cheap and fill up streamers release windows. That is where the joke "nothing good on Netflix" is coming from. People didn't watch it all, its 90% unwatchable slop, and even without ai.

comments.author: dgeisert

I've been in the games industry for 14 years, and I love doing game jams which are making games in a few days or hours.  My fastest game jam game was one hour to make and I was happy with it and played it for about six hours in total after making it.  

I take that view into the AI development as well.  It doesn't have to take a long time to make a great game.  

I'm hosting an AI game jam right now where everyone is building a game within a week period, but the first submissions game in the first day and they are surprisingly good.  The jam is hosted on [itch.io](http://itch.io) if you want to join, and the games will be posted on Friday.  Jam is called Jamference.

People sometimes go on a path of self sabotage for no reason. If the ai creates a mess because you don't use the tool right. Skills are [still a thing](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills), read up how to properly design a project then you will be absolutely fine. 

But that doesn't mean you have all the skills required to finish a game, putting in a state that others want to play it and on top, others want to pay for that game. Copying others will only work for a while, then people realise the clones-of-the-clones aren't as good as the originals. Then creativity, design, "the taste" will get back to the forefront. Millions could shoot real movies with their phone camera but don't. The issue isn't the record button.

comments.author: dJ1fRee
comments.body:
La IA está permitiendo que quienes no sabemos programar pero llevamos toda la vida amando los videojuegos podamos intentar construir aquello que imaginamos. ¿Qué problema hay?  
Innumerables veces, desde niño, he jugado a algo y he pensado: «¿Por qué lo hicieron así y no de esta otra manera?». Antes ahí terminaba la historia. Ahora puedo dedicar mi tiempo, equivocarme, probar, iterar cien veces si hace falta y acabar obteniendo MI propio resultado.  
La IA no me da automáticamente el criterio, las ideas ni la constancia, y desde luego no convierte una mala idea en un buen juego por arte de magia. Pero sí me proporciona herramientas que antes estaban fuera de mi alcance.  
Unos desarrolladores se apoyan en equipos de programadores, artistas, diseñadores y músicos. Los que no tenemos esos recursos podemos apoyarnos también en agentes de IA.  
Luego que el juego sea bueno o malo lo decidirá quien lo juegue. Y me parece perfecto.

comments.author: TheReviewerWildTake
comments.body:
The fact that we are using word "iteration" instead of area specific decisions\\fixes\\masteries - is somewhat telling too.  
  
If players ask to change something, and there is a consensus that "this sucks", they don\`t want to hear "guys, we will iterate until Claude fixes it" - they want to see expertise\\ability to make a surgical, well thought change. 

Unless you are some kind of super beloved indie dev with tons of lovely supporters who for some reason have super high hopes and agree to give you all that time, before moving to the next game - you can\`t rely on something as flimsy as "iterating until it is done"...

comments.author: Material-Database-24
comments.body:
With games (and everything tbh) there are two major factors that really only matter: 1) the idea, and 2) the implementation. There's third, which is price, but we understand that.

Lets immediately put aside the rare exceptions where great idea is made even greater with "bad" implementation like My Summer Car. That game truly thrived in it's early days from glumsy implementation and bugs that added extra spice. That is not the norm.

The norm is that you need both. Great idea and great implementation.

Unfortunately AI does not play in favor for either, quite contradictory. It allows implement bad ideas usually not so greatly. And it allows it super fast and with minimal investment. Hence we are flooded with slop (and that's a fact).

And I can assure you, that once someone makes great game with great implementation with AI, no-one cares it was made with AI. They will still play it and like it.

Consequently, one key factor for success is to get exposure. If your great game never get exposure, no-one finds it and plays it.

This is where the AI slop becomes the key. When you throw out 10000 sloppy ones in a week, the one great is buried under that mass, and it will be mere luck if it finds it's exposure to become widely know.

And that is (IMO) good reason to hate AI slop. And if you are AI game dev, you should also hate it, because if you'd managed to do the great game, it will be unlikely to be found.
